Why raising the minimum wage is all the rage?

Honestly, who wants to work for so little?

But, those pushing companies like McDonalds to increase to their living wage - $15 or more per hour - neglect the economics in this demand. They point to billions in profits each year. GAAP data collected by Morningstar from public financial reports show annual profits of $4.7, $7.5, $6.2, $8.5, and $8.2 billion from 2020 to 2024 prompting the claim from labor leaders that these earnings can be distributed to its workers. 

To assess the impact of such claims, consider a simplified model restaurant chain. This restaurant offers a standard meal at lunch and dinner time for $10.00. The fixed cost amounts to $5.00 per meal (50% of the meal price), the cost of labor is currently $4.50 (45% of the meal price), and the remainder - $0.50 - is profit. Each meal requires 30 minutes of time to prepare by the restaurant staff in line with the $4.50 in labor cost resulting in a $9.00 hourly wage. This restaurant is part of a company that serves 10 million meals each year in 160 restaurants nationwide. Each restaurant of the chain employs 15 workers earning $9.00 each hour for 40 hours a week serve 1200 meals each week. This company employs a total of 2400 workers and is a small capitalization publically traded corporation with 5 million shares valued at $20.00 each and regularly pays a $0.05 each quarter to shareholders. I have $50 to spend at a restaurant each week. My average meal is $10.00 so I can eat at a restaurant five times each week. 

If its labor cost increases from $9.00 to $15.00, and the profit per meal and other cost remain the same. The price of the meal goes from $10.00 to $13.00 and rather than eating there 5 times I can only eat there 4 times for an extra $2.00 each week. The man-hours I contribute as a customer drops from 2.5 hours to 2.0 hours. If the price increase results in a similar trend for regular customers who cannot eat there as often (a 20% drop in sales), only 960 meals are served each week requiring only 12 workers rather than 15 (a total of 480 workers would be let go). Even if a 10% drop in sales, mean one of the 15 workers is let go and one can only work 20 hours a week. A 20% drop in sales corresponds would drop earnings by $1 million dollars and share prices by $4.00 (assuming the price to earnings ratio is the same) resulting in a loss of $20 million in capitalization. 

If the restaurant adjust by making the labor more efficient – my labor cost is the same $4.50, but my purchase only requires 18 minutes (0.30 man-hours). My five weekly purchases drops from 2.5 man-hours to 1.5 man-hours. In this scenario, the profitability of the company is unaffected by this change. However, 1200 meals served each week require 360 rather than 600 man-hours and 9 rather than 15 workers. Only a 66% increase in sales to 2000 meals a week would allow 960 workers to keep their jobs (assuming the remaining workers maintain their previous work week). 

If the restaurant dropped its profit margin from 5% to 1%, it would still need to raise its prices to $12.60 just to cover the additional $3.00 of labor while giving up $0.40 per meal in profit. I would still only be able to eat there 4 times per week for an additional $0.40 each week (as opposed to the $2.00 in an earlier scenario). The loss in sales would still be significant and require the same level of reduction in labor, but the loss of earnings would devastate the stock value. The 20% loss in sales would be compounded by the lower profit margin. The 8 million meals served would net $800,000 in profit or an earnings per share of $0.16 rather than $1.00 earned on $5 million in profit. The stock value would drop to between $4.00 and $5.00 per share with a loss of $75 to $80 million in capitalization. The lower earnings would likely lead to lower dividends ($0.05 twice a year rather than every quarter) or suspension of dividends costing the shareholders between $500,000 and $1 million dollars. 

To this point, the cost of the food prepared is fixed. But, if the wages of one sector rise, the wages of other sectors also rise. The food is the product of the labor of the farmers planting and harvesting the grains, fruits and vegetables, the rancher who raised the cattle and other animals, the baker who made the bread, the butcher who prepared the meat, the condiments maker who prepared the ketchup, mustard and other flavor enhancers, and the railroad engineer and overland truckers who delivered all various ingredients that the cook used to make my meal. If the cook and waiter make 67% more, these other workers would expect at least a similar raise adding say 30% to the food bill’s fixed cost. An increase from $5.00 to $6.50 and my original meal goes from $10.00 to $14.50. Now, $58.00 buys only 4 meals or my food bill for 5 meals is $72.50. The revenue of the company increases from $100 million to $145 million assuming no change in sales even though earnings remain at just $10 million. Meanwhile, the five percent raise of my $20 an hour job means I need to work ten more minutes to afford lunch at the new price of $14.50.
